segments.text: When you type a prompt into ChatGPT, you are sending it a sequence of words.
But the AI doesn't inherently read English.
It needs a mechanism to calculate and extract the precise meaning of the text you provide.
Underneath the interface, the AI splits your text into small pieces, called tokens.
Each token is assigned an embedding, which is a specific row of numbers
that represents its baseline starting meaning.
That starting row of numbers is only a foundation.
To determine what a word actually means in your specific sentence,
the AI has to evaluate the surrounding words, the context.
In this first panel, we see the challenge of ambiguous language.
The word light can mean brightness, as in turn on the light.
Or it can describe weight, as in a suitcase that is light enough to carry.
The second panel shows a similar issue with pronouns.
A single word like it changes its meaning entirely based on the words around it.
It refers to the cat if the cat is thirsty.
But it refers to the milk if the milk is fresh.
The only way to determine which meaning fits is to look at the surrounding words, the context.
While human brains resolve these ambiguities instantly,
for an AI, determining the correct meaning based on context
requires navigating a complex series of mathematical steps.
Historically, solving these contextual ambiguities was a highly inefficient process.
Earlier AI models processed text strictly in sequence,
reading one single word at a time, moving linearly from left to right.
Look at how earlier AI read sentences.
Because it processed words in strict order,
information from cat had to be carried forward step-by-step
down a long, fragile path to define it.
In longer passages, the AI struggled, often losing track of context entirely.
In 2017, a team of researchers at Google published a paper titled
Attention is All You Need.
They introduced a new architecture called the transformer,
which is the T in chat GPT.
This demonstrates how a transformer processes the exact same sentence.
Instead of a linear sequence, the complete message arrives together.
Because tokens are available simultaneously,
AI only draws information from cat,
completely bypassing the distance between them.
However, it forces the AI to actively calculate
exactly which of those simultaneously present words matter for each individual token.
Take a moment and think back to the examples we looked at in the beginning.
See if you can pick out the specific words in those sentences
that lock in the meaning of light or the pronoun it.
Identifying those specific relationships is only the first step.
The AI must then use those connections to mathematically update the row of numbers,
the embedding, that represents the token.
This happens in two main steps, starting with attention.
The attention mechanism calculates relevance
and blends surrounding context directly into the target token's numbers,
feeding data from cat back to it.
Then, transformation applies fixed patterns to process those blended numbers.
The exact numbers representing each token change dramatically during this phase.
Look at the bottom sections of these panels to see the results.
In the first panel, turn on and carry provide context,
signaling the AI to update light for brightness or weight.
It refers to the cat if the cat is thirsty,
but it refers to the milk if the milk is fresh.
By mathematically pulling precise information from relevant words,
the system can interpret complex human phrasing.
These can operate together as the mathematical engine
that builds precise meaning from surrounding text.
This graphic demonstrates why word order is critical.
Dog bites man, and man bites dog use identical tokens for entirely different events.
Without position data, the transformer interprets a scattered cloud of words.
Positional encoding solves this.
By assigning numerical tags to track each word's specific place,
it restores sequential structure.
Attention is all you need.
AI uses relationships between words to help interpret your message.
